body:
Meaning of the Neolithic Age

The Neolithic Age, or New Stone Age, was a major stage in human history during which many communities gradually began producing food by cultivating plants and rearing animals. People continued to use stone tools, but polished stone axes, grinding equipment and other implements became important in several regions.

Earlier hunter-gatherer communities depended mainly on naturally available plants and wild animals. Farming and herding introduced a different relationship with the environment: people could influence which plants grew, which animals reproduced and how some of their food would be obtained in future seasons.

The transition began at different times in different regions. The broad beginnings of domestication are placed around 12,000 years ago, while the Neolithic period is conventionally associated with developments beginning around 10,000 years ago in the wider world. Within the Indian subcontinent, the earliest well-known farming evidence includes Mehrgarh, whose Neolithic occupation began in the 7th millennium BCE.

Neolithic means New Stone Age. In the Indian context, its important features include early agriculture, animal husbandry, polished stone implements and the gradual development of village life. These features did not necessarily appear together at every site.

From Collecting Food to Producing Food

Hunter-gatherers obtained food by hunting animals, fishing and collecting wild fruits, seeds, roots and other plant resources. Their movements often followed seasonal changes in the availability of food and water. Neolithic farmers, by contrast, increasingly planted selected seeds, protected growing crops and collected harvests. Herders managed animals such as sheep, goats and cattle.

Producing food did not mean that hunting and gathering disappeared. Many early farmers continued to hunt, fish and collect wild foods. Some communities combined cultivation with seasonal movement of livestock. A farming settlement could therefore have both a relatively permanent residential area and activities that required people to travel.

Why Farming Encouraged Village Life

Most crops need attention between sowing and harvesting. Farmers must prepare the ground, protect plants, obtain water where necessary and remain available when the grain ripens. Harvested grain can also be saved for later consumption or for sowing in the next season. These requirements encouraged longer stays in suitable locations.

More settled life was accompanied in many areas by houses, storage structures, pottery, grinding stones and activities such as weaving. Over time, settlements could support a greater variety of occupations. However, neither permanent houses nor pottery appeared everywhere at the same moment.

Chronology and Regional Variation

Neolithic, Chalcolithic and Iron Age are useful cultural and technological categories, but they are not rigid dates that apply simultaneously to every part of India. Some communities continued using stone tools while others were already using copper or iron. Their ways of life also differed according to local crops, animals, rainfall and available raw materials.

In many parts of western and central India, regional Chalcolithic farming cultures were important during the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE. Iron became increasingly significant in several regions during the 1st millennium BCE. In northern India, the expansion of early states and towns became particularly visible from around the 6th century BCE.

A change in technology is not the same as an immediate change in society. The appearance of copper did not eliminate stone tools. Similarly, the appearance of iron did not immediately create towns or states in every region.

Prelims focus

  • Neolithic means New Stone Age and is closely associated with early food production.
  • Domestication began gradually, around 12,000 years ago in the broader historical account.
  • Mehrgarh provides important early farming evidence from the 7th millennium BCE.
  • Farming, herding, hunting and gathering could coexist.
  • Trap: Neolithic, Chalcolithic and Iron Age dates were not identical across all Indian regions.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, and Chapter 3, From Gathering to Growing Food, printed pp. 22–31, 2018–19 text; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological Site of Mehrgarh, Tentative List entry 1876, Description, consulted 17 November 2026; INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Module 17, Northwestern, Northern and Northeastern Neolithic of the Indian Subcontinent, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: The Neolithic Age: The Beginning of Food Production

body:
Domestication of Plants

Domestication is the process through which people cultivate selected plants or breed and manage animals over generations, gradually producing forms that differ from their wild ancestors. It is more than simply collecting edible plants or feeding a wild animal once.

Early cultivators could observe that seeds falling on suitable ground produced new plants. By protecting useful plants and saving their seeds, they gradually influenced future harvests. They tended to favour characteristics such as larger grains, stronger stalks and reliable yields. Wheat and barley were among the important early cultivated cereals in the northwestern subcontinent.

Domestication was gradual. A plant did not become fully domesticated in a single season, and the earliest cultivators did not possess the same control over crops that later agricultural societies developed.

Domestication of Animals

Early people probably tamed the wild ancestor of the dog before bringing several food-producing animals under human management. Sheep, goats and cattle became important because they provided meat and, in suitable circumstances, milk and other useful products. Herd management also allowed people to maintain living animals for future use instead of depending entirely on successful hunts.

Animals were selected and bred for useful characteristics, including manageable behaviour. A herd needed access to pasture and water, and animals had to be protected from predators. Consequently, some communities practised a combination of settled agriculture and mobile pastoralism.

Taming concerns the behaviour of an individual animal. Domestication concerns human management and selection over generations. An animal that accepts food from a person is not necessarily a member of a domesticated population.

Tools Used in Farming and Food Preparation

Neolithic communities continued to use stone, wood and bone. The best-known stone implements include polished axes and adzes, which could be useful for cutting or working wood. Other important implements were grinding stones, mortars and pestles, used to process cereals and other plant foods.

The use of polished stone tools distinguishes many Neolithic assemblages from earlier ones dominated by chipped stone tools. Nevertheless, older kinds of tools continued in use, and the presence of a polished axe alone does not establish that every person at a site was a farmer.

Storage, Pottery and Household Activities

Harvested grain had to be protected from moisture, animals and accidental loss. It was also necessary to keep some grain for the following sowing season. Communities used storage pits, baskets, clay containers and purpose-built storage areas according to local circumstances.

Pottery served several purposes. Containers could hold grain, water and other materials, while cooking vessels made it easier to prepare cereals and pulses. The cultivation of plant fibres also supported developments in weaving. Houses, cooking hearths, storage facilities and specialised tools together made village life more varied.

Consequences for Society

A dependable food supply could support larger settlements, but harvests remained vulnerable to drought, floods, disease and pests. Food production therefore created new responsibilities as well as new opportunities.

Village residents might perform different activities, including farming, herding, preparing food, making pots, weaving, constructing shelters and manufacturing tools. Families could cooperate in managing land and animals. These changes helped establish the foundations for later, more complex rural societies without making every Neolithic village socially identical.

Prelims focus

  • Domestication involves selection and management across generations.
  • Wheat and barley were important early domesticated crops.
  • Sheep, goats and cattle were important early managed animals; the dog was an early tamed animal.
  • Polished stone axes, mortars and pestles are important Neolithic tools.
  • Storage was needed for both consumption and future sowing.
  • Trap: The development of agriculture did not immediately end hunting, gathering or seasonal herding.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 3, From Gathering to Growing Food, printed pp. 22–27, 2018–19 text; INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Module 17, sections on Mehrgarh and the Kashmir Neolithic, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Cultivation leads to harvested grain stored in pits, baskets or clay containers, then divided into food and seed saved for the next sowing.
pictures.caption: Saving part of the harvest allowed cultivation to continue into the next season.

title: Domestication, Stone Tools and the Development of Neolithic Villages

body:
Why Regional Traditions Differed

Neolithic communities developed different ways of life because the Indian subcontinent contained contrasting environments. The northwest offered plains suitable for wheat and barley cultivation, Kashmir had cold winters and distinctive dwelling forms, and eastern India offered different crops and ecological conditions.

There was therefore no single Neolithic village pattern that can be applied to all sites. Settlements are identified through combinations of houses, crops, animal remains, tools, pottery and other cultural material.

Mehrgarh: An Early Farming Community

Mehrgarh is situated in the Kachi plain of Balochistan, present-day Pakistan, near the Bolan Pass. It is one of the most important early farming settlements in the northwestern subcontinent.

Its earliest Neolithic occupation belongs to the 7th millennium BCE. Early inhabitants cultivated crops including barley and managed animals such as sheep and goats. Cattle subsequently became especially important. Compartmental mud-brick structures show organised construction and storage activities.

Mehrgarh is particularly useful for understanding gradual change. Its earliest recognised Neolithic phase was aceramic, meaning that pottery was absent from that phase. Ceramic Neolithic and later Chalcolithic phases followed. This shows that farming could develop before the widespread local use of pottery.

Burials have also been identified at Mehrgarh. One burial contained goats placed with the deceased. Such arrangements reveal deliberate treatment of the dead, but the precise beliefs behind them cannot be established with certainty.

Burzahom and Gufkral: The Kashmir Neolithic

Burzahom, near Srinagar in the Kashmir Valley, is known for its pit dwellings. Some houses were constructed by digging below the ground surface, with steps or other means of access. Hearths indicate cooking activities, and the partly underground structures may have offered protection against cold weather. Bone tools were another important feature of the Burzahom assemblage.

Gufkral, also in Kashmir, is notable for an early aceramic Neolithic phase followed by a pottery-using Neolithic phase. Evidence from the Kashmir Neolithic includes cultivation or processing of cereals and pulses, animal management and continued use of wild resources.

Burzahom is the important association for pit houses. Gufkral is especially associated with an early pre-pottery Neolithic phase. Both are in Kashmir.

Neolithic Sites of the Ganga Valley and Eastern India

Koldihwa and Mahagara are associated with the Belan Valley region of present-day Uttar Pradesh. Rice remains are among the important finds from these sites. Mahagara is also associated with evidence of cattle. The occurrence of rice at a site establishes its relevance to early rice use or cultivation; it does not, by itself, establish that rice was first domesticated there.

Chirand, in present-day Bihar, provides evidence of early farming and animal use in the eastern Gangetic region. Finds include grains, animal remains and tools. These sites demonstrate that the early food-producing economy was not restricted to the northwest.

Daojali Hading: The Northeastern Tradition

Daojali Hading is an important Neolithic site in present-day Assam, near routes connected with the Brahmaputra Valley. Stone tools, mortars and pestles, pottery and objects made from fossil wood have been found there.

Jadeite objects are also associated with the site. Their presence suggests possible connections with distant regions, including areas towards present-day China. Such finds are important because they indicate that Neolithic communities were not necessarily isolated.

Prelims focus

  • Mehrgarh is near the Bolan Pass in present-day Pakistan.
  • Mehrgarh has an early pre-pottery Neolithic phase.
  • Burzahom is associated with pit dwellings in Kashmir.
  • Gufkral is associated with an aceramic Neolithic phase.
  • Koldihwa and Mahagara are in Uttar Pradesh; Chirand is in Bihar.
  • Daojali Hading is in Assam and is associated with jadeite finds.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 3, From Gathering to Growing Food, printed pp. 25–30, 2018–19 text; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological Site of Mehrgarh, Tentative List entry 1876, Description, consulted 17 November 2026; INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Module 17, sections on Mehrgarh, the Kashmir-Swat Neolithic, the Belan Valley and northeastern India, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Regional Neolithic Traditions of Northwestern, Northern and Eastern India

body:
The Southern Neolithic Setting

The Neolithic of southern India developed especially across parts of the Deccan Plateau during the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, although individual sites and phases have different dates. It is distinguished by the importance of cattle, polished stone tools, village settlements and regional pottery traditions.

Southern communities adapted to environments that differed from the wheat-barley farming areas of the northwest. Millets and pulses were important crops at several sites. Cattle, sheep, goats and other domestic animals formed part of a mixed agricultural and pastoral economy.

Polished Stone Axes and Pottery

Polished stone axes were important implements in many southern Neolithic settlements. Other tools included grinding stones and smaller stone implements. Pottery was used for storing, cooking and serving food, although shapes and methods of manufacture changed over time and differed from site to site.

Some early pottery was handmade or produced with simple turning methods. Pottery styles are useful for distinguishing regional traditions, but the presence of pottery alone does not establish the exact economic activities of a settlement.

Cattle Keeping and the Ashmound Tradition

One of the most distinctive features of the southern Neolithic is the occurrence of large ashmounds at certain sites. These are extensive accumulations of ash associated with repeated burning of cattle dung that had built up in or near animal-keeping areas.

Ashmounds indicate the importance of cattle management and the repeated use of particular places. The exact reasons for some burning episodes remain uncertain. Burning may have been connected with clearing accumulated dung or with practices of social importance, but a single explanation should not be assumed for every mound.

Utnur, in present-day Telangana, and Budihal, in Karnataka, are important sites associated with the southern Neolithic ashmound tradition.

Important Southern Neolithic Sites

SitePresent stateImportant association
UtnurTelanganaAshmound and cattle-related Neolithic activity
BudihalKarnatakaCattle pens and ashmound evidence
HallurKarnatakaMillets, animals and later cultural developments
PiklihalKarnatakaPastoral Neolithic occupation and pottery
SanganakalluKarnatakaMajor southern Neolithic settlement complex
BrahmagiriKarnatakaNeolithic and later megalithic cultural phases
PaiyampalliTamil NaduNeolithic farming and animal evidence

Hallur is associated with millet and domesticated animals. Paiyampalli is associated with black gram, millet and domestic animals. These examples show that the crops and animals of southern food-producing communities were not identical to those of Mehrgarh.

Links with Later Cultures

Some southern sites contain evidence belonging to more than one cultural period. Brahmagiri, for example, is important for both Neolithic occupation and later megalithic remains. This demonstrates that Neolithic village life and later Iron Age traditions must be understood within a continuing regional history rather than as unrelated developments.

Prelims focus

  • Southern Neolithic communities placed considerable importance on cattle keeping.
  • Ashmounds are strongly associated with repeated burning of accumulated cattle dung.
  • Utnur is in present-day Telangana; Budihal is in Karnataka.
  • Hallur and Brahmagiri are in Karnataka.
  • Paiyampalli is in Tamil Nadu.
  • Trap: An ashmound is not automatically a megalithic burial monument.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 3, From Gathering to Growing Food, site-and-grain table on printed p. 25, 2018–19 text; INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Module 18, Southern Neolithic of India, sections on cattle pastoralism, ashmounds and regional sites, consulted 17 November 2026; INFLIBNET, Module 28, Chalcolithic Cultures of Western India, discussion of the southern Neolithic economy, consulted 17 November 2026.]
